title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.

report.summary: A new arXiv preprint proposes a test-time LLM-agent framework that combines MPPI-style predictive planning with a world model and dual-branch experience memory to improve decisions without extra environment rollouts.
report.background: LLM agents are increasingly expected to act in interactive environments, not just answer questions. Most current agents rely on reactive prompting or chain-of-thought planning, which offers limited lookahead and weak use of accumulated experience. Model-based control offers an alternative: predict outcomes before acting. Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control samples many candidate actions, estimates their costs, and weights them to choose a final action. But language environments rarely provide explicit dynamics or cost functions, making direct MPPI application difficult. This preprint addresses that gap by combining imagined outcomes, heuristic progress and risk scoring, and experience memory that adapts both planning and prediction at test time. It reflects growing interest in inference-time compute and self-improving agents.
key_points: At every decision step, the agent generates multiple candidate actions and uses a learned world model to imagine their likely next observations. This lets it compare alternatives virtually, avoiding costly or risky real environment executions. Because language environments lack explicit dynamics and cost functions, the system scores imagined outcomes by estimated task progress and risk.

The framework borrows MPPI's weighting scheme: candidate actions receive weights based on their predicted costs, and these weighted estimates guide the final choice. This turns planning into a sampling-and-scoring loop rather than a single reactive output, allowing the agent to favor actions that advance the task while limiting risk.

A dual-branch experience memory drives self-improvement. The planner branch stores and reuses successful candidate-generation and action-selection patterns; the world-model branch refines next-observation predictions from accumulated interaction experience. Both branches improve at test time without retraining the backbone, linking planning and prediction.

The authors evaluate on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld with three LLM backbones, reporting strong overall performance and showing that experience-guided predictive control contributes to gains. The abstract does not quantify margins or ablations, and code is promised publicly, so reproducibility and compute overhead remain open questions.
report.impact: The work signals a shift in agent design from single-shot prompting toward inference-time model-based planning. For the AI industry, it supports the idea that reliability can come from better test-time search, world modeling and memory rather than only larger backbones, though it adds latency and compute costs. Developers can adapt the pattern—sample actions, predict outcomes, score progress and risk, then weight—to tool-use and workflow agents, but need reliable evaluators and guardrails. Regular users may see agents that make fewer irreversible mistakes and recover better from feedback, yet such agents will likely be slower and more expensive per task, and benchmark gains do not guarantee open-world safety.
report.tools: Watch the paper's promised code release. For follow-up, explore ALFWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks; MPPI implementations such as pytorch_mppi; world-model frameworks such as DreamerV3; and agent orchestration tools like LangGraph or AutoGen for integrating predictive rollouts and memory. These let developers prototype sampling-based planning, outcome scoring, and dual memory before adopting the full method.
